text: In 1932 Australian soldiers with machine guns were sent to cull emus, and they withdrew after about a month with the birds still roaming free.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 is the shortest recorded war, lasting between 38 and 45 minutes.
In 897 Pope Stephen had the corpse of his predecessor Formosus dug up and put on trial, then cut three fingers off its right hand.
In 1919 a burst tank in Boston sent a wave of molasses through the streets, killing 21 people and injuring 150.
In 1814 a ruptured vat at a London brewery sent a wave of beer into a slum, and eight people died.
In 1518, between 50 and 400 people in Strasbourg danced for weeks, and some of them collapsed.
The Pig War of 1859 between the United States and Britain began when a farmer shot a pig. There were no human casualties, only the pig.
The British war with Spain that began in 1739 is named for Robert Jenkins, a sea captain who said Spanish officials cut off part of his ear.
In 1859 a San Francisco resident named Joshua Norton declared himself Emperor of the United States, and he kept the title until he died in 1880.
In 1943 British agents put a dead man in uniform, with fake plans, into the sea off Spain to make Germany think the Allies would invade Greece and Sardinia.
The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years, though the fighting was on and off.
After Mount Tambora erupted in 1815, 1816 became the Year Without a Summer, and a gloomy holiday that year led Mary Shelley to write Frankenstein.
Hiroo Onoda kept up guerrilla warfare on a Philippine island until 1974, because he and his men did not believe the flyers saying World War II was over.
Tsutomu Yamaguchi survived both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bombings in 1945.
Violet Jessop survived the sinking of the Titanic and the Britannic, and she was aboard their sister ship Olympic when it collided with a warship.
A blast over Siberia in 1908 flattened nearly 2,150 square kilometres of forest in a radial pattern.
During the huge 1859 solar storm, telegraph pylons threw sparks, some operators got shocks, and others kept sending messages with their power switched off.
In the 1904 Olympic marathon, the winner's trainers gave him brandy, raw eggs and strychnine, and he finished hallucinating.
Tug of war was an Olympic team event at every Games from 1900 to 1920.
From 1912 to 1948, the Olympic Games included art competitions.
The pits of the Terracotta Army hold more than 8,000 soldiers, and their faces appear to be different for each figure.
On his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, Mali's Mansa Musa gave away so much gold that it is said to have shaken the metal's value in Cairo.
In 1805 the pirate fleet of Zheng Yi, later led by his widow Zheng Yi Sao, had about 400 junks and between 40,000 and 70,000 pirates.
In 1618 two royal governors and their secretary were thrown from a Prague castle window, survived the 21-metre fall, and the incident helped spark a long war.
Peter the Great ordered Russian boyars to shave their beards, and those who kept them had to pay an annual beard tax of 100 rubles.
Around Christmas 1914, soldiers on parts of the Western Front stopped fighting, swapped small gifts, and in places played football against each other.
The Swedish warship Vasa sank about 1,300 metres into her maiden voyage in 1628, and was raised from the seabed in 1961.
In World War II the US Ghost Army fooled German forces with inflatable tanks, sound trucks and fake radio transmissions.
China's 1958 campaign against sparrows killed at least 200 million of them, and it is counted among the causes of the Great Chinese Famine.
In 1962 Soviet officer Vasily Arkhipov is credited with preventing the launch of a nuclear torpedo from a submarine during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
In 1983 Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov judged a missile warning to be a false alarm, and that choice may have helped avoid a nuclear war.
Some of Stonehenge's stones, the bluestones, were brought there from Wales.
In 1889 and 1890 reporter Nellie Bly went around the world in 72 days, in imitation of Phileas Fogg from Jules Verne's novel.
Philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein inherited a fortune and gave it away, part to poets and artists and the rest to his siblings.
The Great Stink of 1858 was a summer when the Thames smelled so foul that it pushed London toward building a new sewer system.
Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, with its carved stone pillars, was inhabited from around 9500 BCE, long before pottery was in use there.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was the world's tallest human-made structure for more than 3,700 years.
By 1987 an estimated 33,000 people lived in Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong, on a site of only 2.6 hectares.
Robert Wadlow, the tallest person on record, stood 2.72 metres, or 8 feet 11 inches, tall.
Film star Hedy Lamarr co-invented a radio guidance system for torpedoes that used frequency hopping, an idea later used in Bluetooth and early Wi-Fi.
Jeanne Calment of France reached 122 years and 164 days, the longest verified human lifespan.
Marie Curie's notebooks are expected to stay radioactive for well over a thousand years, because of the radium-226 they carry.
After Israel's first president died in 1952, Albert Einstein was offered the job. He declined.
Isaac Newton was Master of the Royal Mint in London for years, where he worked to punish coin clippers and counterfeiters.
Astronomer Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in a sword duel at age 20 and wore a prosthetic nose, later found to be made of brass.
Told that the taxi number 1729 was dull, mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan said it was the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two ways.
Mathematician Paul Erdős published around 1,500 papers, many of them written with other mathematicians.
Grigori Perelman proved the Poincaré conjecture, then rejected the one-million-dollar prize offered for it.
Cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 without her knowledge became the HeLa line, the first immortalized human cell line.
Wilhelm Röntgen refused to take out patents on X-rays, because he wanted society as a whole to benefit.
Most of Leonardo da Vinci's writings are in mirror-image cursive, probably because he wrote with his left hand.
Ada Lovelace wrote an algorithm for Babbage's Analytical Engine, and she is often called the first computer programmer.
Erik Satie's Vexations is a piano piece that his manuscript implies should be played over and over, 840 times.
John Cage's 4'33" tells performers not to play their instruments for the whole piece, which lasts four minutes and 33 seconds.
Agatha Christie's The Mousetrap opened in London's West End in 1952 and is the longest-running show there, with over 30,000 performances.
Vatican City, at about 0.49 square kilometres, is the smallest country in the world by area.
Kiribati's atolls stretch into the northern, southern, eastern and western hemispheres.
The point in the ocean farthest from land is so remote that the closest humans are sometimes astronauts on the International Space Station.
The shores of the Dead Sea are the lowest land on Earth, about 440 metres below sea level.
Lesotho is the only independent country in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 metres in elevation.
Nauru, a Pacific island country of 21 square kilometres, has no official capital, but its government sits in Yaren.
Bhutan has long put Gross National Happiness at the centre of its policy goals, instead of just economic growth.
A gas-filled crater in Turkmenistan has been on fire since 1971.
Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world, and it sits on brine that is rich in lithium.
The Danube passes through or touches the borders of ten countries, more than any other river.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, with a height of 979 metres.
Some weather stations in Chile's Atacama Desert have never received any rain.
Tristan da Cunha, a group of volcanic islands in the South Atlantic, is considered the most remote inhabited place in the world.
Finland has at least two million saunas, and perhaps over three million, for a population of about 5.5 million.
Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport lies about 4.5 metres below sea level.
A Welsh village on Anglesey has a 58-letter name, reputed to be the longest place name in Europe.
A hill in New Zealand has an 85-letter Maori name, and it is often cited as the longest place name in the world.
Since 1967 an old sea fort off Britain, Roughs Tower, has been claimed as the Principality of Sealand, a micronation that no country recognizes.
Ecuador's Chimborazo is not the highest mountain, but its summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's centre.
Measured from its base under the ocean, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is called the tallest mountain in the world by some authorities.
Lake Hillier, off the coast of Western Australia, is known for its pink colour.
Istanbul is a city on two continents: about two thirds of its people live in Europe and the rest in Asia.
Iceland was essentially free of mosquitoes until October 2025.
The oldest bristlecone pine is more than 4,800 years old, the oldest known individual of any species.
Pando, a grove of quaking aspens in Utah, is one clonal organism with about 47,000 stems, weighing an estimated 6,000 tonnes.
Longyearbyen on Svalbard has a polar night of 111 days, from 27 October to 15 February, and the town is home to a global seed vault.
Kolmanskop in Namibia's Namib desert was once a rich diamond-mining village, and it is now a ghost town.
Hashima Island in Japan had a peak population of 5,259 in 1959, and was emptied in 1974 when its coal mine closed.
The volcanic island of Surtsey, off Iceland, reached the sea surface in November 1963 and its eruption lasted until 1967.
Siberia's Lake Baikal is the largest freshwater lake in the world by volume, holding over a fifth of the planet's fresh surface water.
Challenger Deep, the deepest known point of the seabed, is about 10,900 to 11,000 metres down.
During the African humid period, much of the Sahara was covered by grasses, trees and lakes.
Liechtenstein is doubly landlocked, meaning that every country it borders is itself landlocked.
Zealandia, the area around New Zealand, is an almost entirely submerged mass of continental crust.
Lake Vostok in Antarctica is a fresh water lake that lies about 4,000 metres below the surface of the ice.
Bir Tawil, a stretch of land between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither country.
The Belgian town of Baarle-Hertog is scattered in pieces inside the Netherlands, and some of those pieces contain small Dutch enclaves.
To a botanist a banana is a berry, but a strawberry is not.
A single rotation of Venus, 243 Earth days, takes longer than its 224.7 day trip around the Sun.
Water has a triple point at 0.01 degrees Celsius, where ice, liquid water and vapour can exist together.
Helium was first seen as a yellow line in sunlight during an eclipse in 1868, before anyone had found it on Earth.
Lightning strikes Earth about 44 times every second, nearly 1.4 billion flashes a year.
Nutmeg is a spice that in high doses can cause hallucinations, and in larger amounts serious poisoning.
The banana equivalent dose is an informal unit of radiation, based on the radioactive potassium naturally found in a banana.
Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a lump of it will melt in your hand.
Deep inside Uranus, extreme pressure may squeeze carbon into diamonds that rain down through the planet's mantle.
Saturn is the only planet in the Solar System that is less dense than water.
The Queensland pitch drop experiment began in 1927 and a drop forms only about every 12 to 13 years; in 2000 nobody saw it fall.
Neptune finished its first full orbit of the Sun since its discovery in 1846 only in July 2011.
The Mpemba effect is the observation that very hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cooler water.
In 1986 Lake Nyos in Cameroon suddenly released a cloud of carbon dioxide that suffocated 1,746 people and 3,500 livestock.
In the 1950s a fungus nearly wiped out the Gros Michel banana, and the Cavendish took its place as the main variety.
Auroras are not just an Earth thing: ultraviolet auroras have also been seen on Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
In a group of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is better than 50 percent.
Graham's number is so huge that the observable universe is too small to hold its digits if you tried to write it out.
A hexagon-shaped cloud pattern circles Saturn's north pole, and each of its sides is longer than Earth is wide.
Olympus Mons on Mars is about 2.5 times as high as Mount Everest is above sea level, and it is the tallest volcano on that planet.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot was first observed in 1831, and over the past century it has been shrinking.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes of liquid hydrocarbons in its polar regions.
Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active world in the Solar System.
The Sun makes up about 99.86 percent of the total mass of the Solar System.
Crushing Wint-O-Green Life Savers in the dark gives off little sparks, an effect called triboluminescence.
Superfluid liquid helium can creep up the walls of its container and siphon itself out against gravity.
From 1889 until 2019 the kilogram was defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder kept in France.
In 1791 the French National Assembly declared that the metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole.
A 1750 act of Parliament removed eleven days from September 1752 as Britain switched to the Gregorian calendar.
In 1844 the Philippines went straight from Monday 30 December to Wednesday 1 January, skipping a day, to join the Asian side of the date line.
Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis, 45 letters long, is the longest word in a popular English dictionary.
The Rotokas language of Papua New Guinea is written with only 12 letters of the Latin alphabet.
The Taa language of Botswana and Namibia has perhaps the largest number of phonemes of any language, with many click consonants.
Silbo Gomero is a whistled form of Spanish used on La Gomera in the Canary Islands.
Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country in the world, with about 840 living languages.
Basque is Europe's only known language isolate, with no known relation to any other language.
The word robot comes from the 1920 Czech play R.U.R., and may have been coined by the author's brother, Josef.
The word mondegreen, for a misheard phrase, was coined by the writer Sylvia Wright in 1954.
The ampersand was once regarded as the 27th letter of the English alphabet.
The Voynich manuscript is a 15th-century illustrated book written in a script nobody has been able to read.
Linear A, a script used on ancient Crete, has never been deciphered.
Nushu, meaning women's script, was a syllabic writing used in Jiangyong county in Hunan, China.
Nicaraguan Sign Language was developed by deaf children brought together in several schools in Nicaragua.
A 1934 Merriam-Webster dictionary defined 'dord' as a synonym for density, but the word was an error and never really existed.
In Iceland most people use a patronymic, based on a parent's first name, rather than a family name, and a naming committee approves new first names.
Esperanto was created by L. L. Zamenhof in 1887 as a language for the world to share.
The word OK likely comes from a fashion in the late 1830s for abbreviating misspellings, as in 'oll korrect' for 'all correct'.
The Sator Square is a Latin word square containing a five-word palindrome, and copies have been found at Roman-era sites.
People tend to match the made-up word 'kiki' with a spiky shape, and 'bouba' with a rounded one.
The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created at the urging of King Sejong the Great and officially published in 1446.
Sequoyah invented the Cherokee syllabary in the late 1810s and early 1820s to write the Cherokee language.
The Klingon language, spoken by aliens in Star Trek, was described by Marc Okrand in a 1985 dictionary.
Toki Pona is a constructed language built around only about 120 to 137 words.
The Inca kept records on quipu, devices made of knotted cords.
One of the first emoji sets, for a Japanese mobile service in 1999, was designed by Shigetaka Kurita.
The interrobang, a mark that combines a question mark with an exclamation mark, was first proposed in 1962 by Martin K. Speckter.
Cuneiform writing first appears in Uruk at the end of the fourth millennium BC, made with a stylus on clay.
The word petrichor, for the smell of rain on dry ground, was introduced by two Australian researchers in a 1964 paper.
A light bulb in a California fire station was first lit in 1901 and has been turned off only a few times since.
Post-it Notes use a low-tack adhesive, which came from a 3M scientist's failed 1968 try at a super-strong glue.
Engineer Percy Spencer noticed that radar equipment was melting a candy bar in his pocket, which led to the microwave oven.
Swiss engineer George de Mestral thought of Velcro after burrs from burdock kept sticking to his dog's fur and his clothes.
A Rubik's Cube can be arranged in about 43 quintillion different ways.
The world's first webcam was pointed at a coffee pot in the Computer Laboratory at the University of Cambridge.
The first item ever scanned at a store checkout was a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum, in Troy, Ohio, in 1974.
The Antikythera mechanism, found in a Greek shipwreck, is an ancient geared device that could predict astronomical positions and eclipses.
The Lycurgus Cup, from Roman times, looks red when light shines through it and green when lit from the front, thanks to gold and silver nanoparticles.
Heat from the sun can make the top of the Eiffel Tower lean away from it by up to 18 centimetres.
Nokia, the phone company, began in 1865 as a pulp mill.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 to make handmade hanafuda playing cards.
The teddy bear is named after US President Theodore Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a captured bear on a hunting trip in 1902.
Monopoly was inspired by The Landlord's Game, a board game patented in 1904 by Elizabeth Magie to teach about land and taxes.
Bluetooth is named for the 10th-century Danish king Harald Bluetooth, who united the Danish tribes into one kingdom.
Hawaiian pizza was invented in Chatham, Ontario, in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek-born Canadian.
The Shigir Idol, a carved wooden figure found in Russia, is about 11,500 years old and is the oldest known wooden sculpture.
The Voyager spacecraft each carry a golden record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, plus music and sounds of Earth.
Alexander Bain patented an electric printing telegraph in 1843, an early fax-type machine, decades before the telephone.
The Slinky was invented in 1943 by naval engineer Richard T. James.
Bubble Wrap began as an attempt to make a three-dimensional plastic wallpaper, and when that failed it became packing material.
The name WD-40 stands for Water Displacement, 40th formula, because it was the fortieth try at the recipe.
The first Ferris wheel was built for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago to rival the Eiffel Tower.
The theremin is an electronic instrument played without touching it, by moving the hands near two metal antennas.
Mr. Potato Head, first sold by Hasbro in 1952, was the first toy advertised on television.
Sony executive Norio Ohga reportedly wanted the compact disc to be big enough to hold all of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.
The Wilhelm scream, a stock sound effect, started with the 1951 film Distant Drums and has turned up in many films since.
An octopus has three hearts.
Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings.
Tardigrades, tiny animals also called water bears, have survived being exposed to outer space.
The wood frog survives winter by letting 65 to 70 percent of the water in its body freeze.
After his owner died, the Akita dog Hachiko went to Tokyo's Shibuya Station almost every day for nearly ten years, hoping to meet him.
Stubbs the cat was the honorary mayor of Talkeetna, Alaska, from 1997 until he died in 2017.
Honey bees use a waggle dance to share information about food with the rest of the hive.
The axolotl can regenerate body parts, including limbs, gills and even parts of its eyes and brain.
Cher Ami, a homing pigeon, is said to have delivered a message in 1918 that saved the Lost Battalion, despite being shot through the breast.
Crows can recognize and remember individual human faces.
Three-toed sloths climb down to the ground about once a week to go to the toilet, digging a hole and covering it afterwards.
Wojtek, a bear adopted by Polish soldiers in World War II, is said to have carried ammunition crates at the Battle of Monte Cassino.
